chunks: Al-Bazofari from Ahmad ibn Idris, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Abdillah ibn al-Mughira, from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from al-'Ala' ibn Razin, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

In the case of a man who manumitted conditionally (dabbara) a slave of his, and the slave ran away (abaq) and went to a people and married among them, and he did not inform them that he was a slave, and children were born to him and he acquired wealth, and the master who had manumitted him died. Then the heirs of the deceased who had manumitted the slave came and sought the slave. He was asked: What do you think? He said: 'The slave and his children belong to the heirs of the deceased.' I said: 'Has he not already been manumitted conditionally?' He replied: 'When he ran away, it invalidated his manumission, and he returned to slavery.'

key_terms.أَبَقَ: To run away or escape from slavery

ai.seo_question: What happens to a conditionally manumitted slave's status and property if he runs away before the master dies?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the legal mechanism of 'haram' (breaking) in conditional manumission (*tadbir*), establishing that a slave's flight (*abq*) nullifies the emancipation contract, reverting him to slavery. Consequently, upon the master's death, the heirs retain ownership not only of the slave but also of his offspring and acquired wealth, a ruling derived from Imam al-Sadiq's (AS) explanation that the act of running away effectively demolishes the status of freedom. This principle underscores the dynamic nature of *tadbir* in Shia jurisprudence, where the condition of freedom is contingent upon the slave's compliance rather than being an immediate, irrevocable transfer of status.
